messages.body_plain:
Solomon (list)

I've placed my answer to Solomon's question in the Disqus forum where he asked the question.  He asked his question a second time to this list, but I've answered it in its original location (https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/contact/)

I intend to answer questions raised from the online course at the online course web pages.

---

Solomon

Really happy to hear you are getting good use out of the online materials.  That's why we posted them.

You ask a good question about the meaning of "A" defined as the size of the region of interest.  This can often be a source of confusion for researchers.  The short answer to your question is A=21.2km^2.

This is because you only sampled one stratum of the park, all of your transects were located in that stratum.  Consequently, you cannot make inference to the remaining strata in the park because your study design made it impossible for sampling effort (transects) to fall into the remaining strata.  Your study will allow you to make inference about only the stratum where you sampled.  Consequently, the "size of the region of interest" in your study is the size if that single stratum, not the size of the entire park.

Let us know if you have more questions.

"In coastal surveys, the horizon is often obscured by land. In this case, the observer measures the declination from the shoreline to the sighting (using binocular reticles) while the vessel’s captain simultaneously measures the distance to the shoreline in the same direction via RADAR (a laser-range finder can also be used if close to shore). In analysis, you can add the expected declination (in reticles) from the horizon to the shoreline given its distance to your observed declination, and then convert this total declination to a true distance to the animals (e.g. Barlow, 1995; Lerczak & Hobbs, 1998). Distance to land can also be measured from the boat position (if that is known accurately, e.g. via GPS) using accurate paper or digital charts. Even inexpensive, hand-held GPS units are accurate enough for this purpose without differential correction (e.g. Garmin eTrex; over 48 hours 50% of fixes were <3.8 m of the true position, and 95% were <6.7 m; Wilson, 2007)."  Dawson, Steve; Wade, Paul; Slooten, Elisabeth; and Barlow, Jay, "Design and field methods for sighting surveys of cetaceans in coastal and riverine habitats" (2008). Publications, Agencies and Staff of the U.S. Department of Commerce. 255. http://digitalcommons.unl.edu/usdeptcommercepub/255

messages.body_plain:
Malene

The issue causing the warning is adjustment terms.  Warnings are issued by Distance with the programme has two instructions it is trying to perform, but those instructions are in conflict.  In this case the instructions are to a) achieve the best fit to the data and b) not have a fitted detection function that increases as a function of distance.  Warnings do not necessarily indicate problems as much as suggestions to look deeper into the fitting process.

These add flexibility to the key function models, and permit the fitted detection function to have wiggles in it.  Sometimes those wiggles cause the detection to rise, rather than fall, over some distance range.  When the detection function rises, this violates the principle of monotonicity--that a detection function should only decrease as a function of distance.

When analysing your data from animal groups as individuals, this will invariably cause some "lumps" in your data that the models with adjustments may be trying to fit.  Besides the AIC score, you ought also to be examining the goodness of fit statistic.  You might expect some poorer fit caused by the lumps in your sightings, but assess the absolute fit of your models (via goodness of fit tests) in addition to assessing relative fit (via AIC).

Malene

Comparison of AIC across datasets (individuals vs clusters) is uninformative and will not serve as a guide to the best way to proceed.

I think you find yourself in a position of compromise; analysing data as groups has less over-dispersion in the histogram of distances and hence a better fit.  However you are uncomfortable with the measure of group size and location of group centre.

To circumvent the issues of group size measurement, data can be analysed as individuals.  This brings in the over-dispersion and subsequent deterioration in model fit metrics.  I'm afraid this is as far as objectivity in analysis can take you.  From this point you must reconcile which of the compromises you prefer.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Reading through this example:

http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html

... the final summary states:

Pooled detection function

Estimates of group abundance when a detection function is fitted to data pooled across strata. These results are actually incorrect because effort was not equally allocated between the strata. The southern stratum is much smaller (84000km2) than the northern (630000km2). But the southern stratum is more desirable habitat for the minke whales because it is closer to the ice edge in Antarctica. The southern stratum had much greater survey effort per area than the northern stratum. This is not represented in the pooled analysis.

If I understand correctly, the results are incorrect because the detection function will be biased towards fitting the data from the stratum with more observations, at the expense of fit to the less-observations stratum. The density estimate for the two areas would be affected, so despite accounting for the area when multiplying up from the density estimate (and despite the density estimate accounting for survey effort), the abundance estimates would be wrong.

Am I right in thinking this is only the case when the detection function is different between strata? If we imagine a case where the detectability is identical between two strata, and thus the detection function is identical if fitted separately or pooled, this would not affect the density estimates, even if the area and effort is different? (Of course, the abundance estimate would differ if the area differed).

Dear Don,

You are correct in that you cannot define adjustment terms in the make.detectability function to specify the detection function used to generate the data. However, you can define a hazard rate detection function where the scale parameter is affected by covariates. Please find an example below where the scale parameter varies with cluster size.

library(DSsim)
covariate.list <- list()
covariate.list$size <- list(list("ztruncpois", list(mean = 5)))
pop <- make.population.description(covariates = covariate.list)

covariate.params <- list(size = 0.1)
detect <- make.detectability(key.function = 'hr',
                             shape.param = 1,
                             cov.param = covariate.params)

plot(detect, pop)

Best wishes,

messages.body_plain:
Luke, that comment from the paper makes no sense at all.  It suggests the writer is completely ignorant of the issue of sampling variation!  TRANSECT probably would have quite happily modelled those data.  TRANSECT had only the Fourier series model (uniform key + cosine adjustments in Distance parlance).  It fitted the model by method of moments, while Distance fits using maximum likelihood.  Yes, Distance has much more flexibility, but no, it would not be right to say that it would model these data adequately, but TRANSECT could not.  The fault is not with TRANSECT but with the statement in the paper.

Steve Buckland
